content:
For \(n=1\), the polygon is a triangle. Color its three sides with the three colors; from any exterior point, at most two sides of a triangle are visible, so this works.

Now assume \(n\ge 2\). We show no such coloring exists.

**Fact 1.** Any \(n+1\) consecutive sides of a regular \((2n+1)\)-gon can be seen from some exterior point.  
Indeed, the outward normals of \(n+1\) consecutive sides lie in an arc of length
\[
n\cdot \frac{2\pi}{2n+1}<\pi.
\]
Taking an exterior point far away in the middle direction of this arc makes exactly those \(n+1\) sides visible.

**Fact 2.** In any \(3\)-coloring of the sides of a regular \((2n+1)\)-gon, \(n\ge 2\), using all three colors, some \(n+1\) consecutive sides have all three colors.

Suppose not: every block of \(n+1\) consecutive sides misses at least one color. For each cyclic block \(W_i=\{i,i+1,\dots,i+n\}\), choose a missing color \(c_i\). The \(c_i\) cannot all be the same, because then that color would appear nowhere. So for some \(i\), \(c_i\ne c_{i+1}\). Let \(c_i=X\), \(c_{i+1}=Y\), and let \(Z\) be the third color.

Then \(W_i\) uses only \(Y,Z\), and \(W_{i+1}\) uses only \(X,Z\). Their intersection is \(n\) consecutive sides, all colored \(Z\). Number these \(Z\)-colored sides \(1,\dots,n\). The remaining \(n+1\) consecutive sides \(n+1,\dots,2n+1\) must contain all occurrences of \(X\) and \(Y\), so they contain at least one \(X\) and one \(Y\). If they also contained \(Z\), they would already be a block of \(n+1\) consecutive sides with all three colors, impossible. Hence they contain only \(X,Y\). Moreover, side \(n+1\) must be \(X\), and side \(2n+1\) must be \(Y\).

Thus the block \(n+1,\dots,2n+1\) is a sequence of only \(X,Y\), starting with \(X\) and ending with \(Y\). So there is an adjacent pair \(k,k+1\) inside it with different colors. If \(k=n+1\), then the block \(n,n+1,\dots,2n\) contains \(Z,X,Y\). If \(k\ge n+2\), then the block \(k,k+1,\dots,k+n\) wraps around and contains a \(Z\)-colored side, together with \(X\) and \(Y\). In either case, some \(n+1\) consecutive sides contain all three colors, contradiction.

Therefore, for \(n\ge 2\), some exterior point sees all three colors, so the coloring is impossible.

Hence the largest possible positive integer is \(\boxed{1}\).
